# Introduction

Storage is the reflexive response to drought, and the evidence that it is keeping up is
weakening. Global reservoir capacity keeps growing through new construction, yet the fraction of
that capacity actually holding water has declined [@li_diminishing_2023], and of 525 large
reservoirs tracked by satellite altimetry between 2010 and 2022, 93% failed to fill at least
once, with those in significant decline concentrated in the Southern Hemisphere between 14° and
44° S [@wang_reservoir_2024]. Whether more storage is the right answer turns on how much drought relief a
reservoir delivers, as opposed to appearing to deliver because of where it was built. Dams are not sited at random.
They are built where water is scarce and demand is high, often in direct response to the damage
of a previous shortage [@di_baldassarre_water_2018], under economic and political pressures that
select particular basins [@kellner_controversial_2021]. Dammed basins are therefore drier and
more water dependent than the undammed basins they are compared against before any drought
begins, so the contrast mixes the effect of the dam with the reason the dam is there.

What reservoirs do at short timescales is reasonably well established. Operations shorten and
soften hydrological drought at one to three month accumulations [@wu_non-linear_2017;
@wu_impacts_2018], and inflow-based counterfactuals find that regulation delays drought
downstream [@wu_assessing_2019; @wu_reservoirs_2021; @wan_hydrological_2017]. The multi-year timescale is where the evidence thins and the stakes
rise. The same analyses that resolve short-term buffering report that the effect on 12 and 24
month drought is not apparent [@wu_impacts_2018], dam drought resistance weakens or disappears
as events intensify [@lee_drought_2026], and even a reservoir holding two years of mean annual
flow mitigates decadal variability while leaving the rarest and deepest shortages largely
untouched [@ho_future_2017]. Under structural aridification it is the multi-year deficit that
decides whether storage protects anyone.

Settling the question requires a counterfactual, what the basin's drought would have been
without the dam, and each of the approaches in use leaves the siting problem partly open.
Model-based and naturalized-flow reconstructions read regulation against simulated unregulated
flow, but inherit the model's memory, and conceptual storage models cannot accumulate
deficits across years [@AlvarezGarreton2021], so the counterfactual is weakest at the timescale
of interest.
Before-and-after and regulated-versus-natural comparisons avoid the model but not the confound,
since regulated and near-natural catchments are not distributed homogeneously across
hydroclimatic zones, so climate imprints directly on the estimated regulation effect, as such
studies note themselves [@gotte_hydrological_2024]. Paired-gauge designs come closest, reading a
regulated reach against an unregulated reference [@lopezmoreno_dam_2009], and have been scaled
nationally to flow-regime alteration [@chalise_dams_2021; @chalise_spectral_2023], but not to
multi-year drought transmission conditional on the deficit each basin actually experienced. The
field that framed the reservoir effect says as much: the tools to quantify the long-term
dynamics of storage are still missing [@di_baldassarre_water_2018].

We therefore build the counterfactual inside the basin. If a dam buffers drought, the
transmission of meteorological deficit into streamflow deficit must flatten below the dam, where
releases are managed, and not above it, where they are not. Reaches above and below the same dam
share climate, geology, and the entire history that put a dam there, so differencing them
removes siting without invoking a model, and if the attenuation is equally present upstream it
is a property of the location rather than of the operation. This upstream/downstream placebo is
our central identification strategy. We pair it with a matched cross-basin comparison against hydroclimatically comparable undammed basins,
evaluating both against the drought each actually experienced rather than calendar time, which
breaks the collinearity between megadrought onset and treatment.
The estimand throughout is impact per unit of deficit, at annual to multi-year accumulation, the
timescale of structural drought rather than of seasonal operation.

Chile is an acute testbed. Since 2010 its central regions have endured a *megadrought*, an
uninterrupted run of dry years shading into structural aridification with a documented
anthropogenic component [@garreaud_20102015_2017; @Garreaud2025; @zambrano_drought_2025;
@Boisier2018; @vicenteserrano_unraveling_2019], and it sits in the band where reservoir levels
are falling fastest worldwide [@wang_reservoir_2024]. The
1981 Water Code makes water-use rights perpetual private property, so the policy reflex has been
supply-side, new dams and inter-basin transfers, alongside market incentives that concentrated
water in high-value export crops [@Barria2021; @reade_malagueno_libre_2024;
@rivera_legal_2016]. In the snow-fed basins of central Chile demand
already outruns supply in roughly three years of every ten [@webb_water_2021]. Chile thus
exhibits every ingredient of the reservoir effect, making it a most-likely case for detecting
one if it operates, and its short, steep Andean catchments, gauged above and below major dams,
provide the physical setup the upstream placebo requires.

We adjudicate two accounts of the attenuated transmission that dammed basins have been reported
to show, and bound what the data can decide between them. Under
operational buffering the attenuation is a regulation effect, so it should appear below dams and
not at the unregulated reaches above them, persist when dammed basins are compared within their
own climate regime, and concentrate in the reservoirs with enough storage to carry water across
years. Under siting it is a property of location, equally present upstream and dissolving once
the aridity gradient along which reservoirs are sited is removed. The reservoir-effect
hypothesis adds a demand-side prediction that runs against buffering altogether, that if storage
induces the expansion it is built to serve, dammed basins should accumulate irrigated land and
water claims faster through a prolonged drought. We test these predictions across the
streamflow, cropland, and water-rights pathways with pre-specified falsifiers, and report the
minimum detectable effect alongside every estimate, since a failure to reject is only as
informative as the effect it can exclude.
